usage: 성격 (personality) is the noun it pairs with most
-(이)라서 gives a reason off a 이다-adjective
I'd say I'm on the introverted side
-(으)ㄴ 편이다 hedges instead of stating it flatly
Habitually chained with 조용하다 in self-descriptions
examples: 저는 좀 내성적이에요.
I'm a bit introverted.
Add 좀 to soften a self-label; note the form is 내성적이에요, not 내성적해요
저는 내성적이라서 처음 보는 사람이랑 말하는 게 어려워요.
I'm introverted, so talking to people I'm meeting for the first time is hard.
-(이)라서 links the trait to its everyday consequence
걔는 내성적이지만 친해지면 말이 엄청 많아.
He's introverted, but once you get close he talks a ton.
걔 + banmal among friends; -지만 sets up the contrast
nuance: 내성적이다 is the neutral, textbook word for 'introverted' and is completely safe to say about yourself in interviews or first meetings — Koreans read it as a temperament, not a flaw. It is Sino-Korean: 內省的 (內 inner + 省 to reflect/introspect), literally 'inward-reflecting type', so it points to drawing energy inward rather than to being unfriendly. The key contrast is with 소심하다 (timid), which adds a negative 'holds back out of fear' edge, and with 조용하다 (quiet), which is only about low volume; an introvert can be talkative once comfortable. It collocates with 성격, 사람, and the hedge -(으)ㄴ 편이다. The pitfall for English speakers is the conjugation: because the stem already ends in 이다, you say 내성적이에요 / 내성적인, never the 하다-style 내성적해요.

mistakes: Saying 내성적해요 — there is no 하다 here; the stem is 내성적이다, so it conjugates as 내성적이에요 / 내성적인
Treating it as a synonym of 소심하다 — 내성적 is just inward-facing and value-neutral, while 소심하다 implies timid, fearful holding-back
Using it to mean merely 'quiet' (조용하다) — composure and volume are separate; 내성적 is about where you get your energy

usage: 외향적으로 + 변하다 = change in that direction
-(으)ㄴ 편이다 to hedge rather than declare
examples: 저는 외향적이에요.
I'm outgoing.
Basic self-intro; the form is 외향적이에요, never 외향적해요
저는 외향적이라서 새 친구 사귀는 게 좋아요.
I'm outgoing, so I enjoy making new friends.
친구를 사귀다 = make friends; -(이)라서 ties trait to behavior
우리 팀장님은 진짜 외향적이라서 회식 때 분위기를 다 살려요.
Our team lead is super outgoing, so they liven up the whole mood at company dinners.
분위기를 살리다 = liven up the mood; a 회식 staple scene
nuance: 외향적이다 is the standard, positive-leaning term for 'extroverted' and is woven into MBTI chat, which is hugely popular in Korea — you will constantly hear 'E야 I야?' (Are you an E or an I?). It is Sino-Korean: 外向的 (外 outside + 向 to face/turn toward), literally 'outward-facing type', describing where someone aims their energy. The sharp contrast is with 활발하다: 외향적이다 names the inner trait, while 활발하다 describes the visible liveliness you can see in a room — an extrovert who happens to be tired won't look 활발한 at that moment. It pairs with 성격, the verb 변하다 (외향적으로 변하다), and the hedge -(으)ㄴ 편이다. The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't add 하다 (it's 외향적이에요 / 외향적인), and don't swap in the noun 외향성 (extroversion) where the adjective belongs — say 외향적이에요, not 외향성이에요.

usage: 꼼꼼하게 = adverb form; collocates strongly with 확인하다
High praise for a coworker's reliability
Frequently listed as a 장점 (strength) in interviews
꼼꼼히 = alternate adverb, a touch more written
examples: 이거 꼼꼼하게 확인했어?
Did you check this thoroughly?
Everyday office question; 꼼꼼하게 modifies 확인하다
저 사람 일 진짜 꼼꼼하게 해서 실수가 거의 없어.
That person works so meticulously they almost never make mistakes.
Casual praise; 실수 = mistake
메뉴를 꼼꼼하게 읽어 보고 시키세요.
Read the menu carefully before you order.
Practical everyday advice; 꼼꼼하게 modifies 읽어 보다 ('read and check')
nuance: 꼼꼼하다 is native Korean for being careful, thorough, and reliable with details, and in a work context it is high, almost unambiguous praise — it is one of the safest 'strengths' to claim in a Korean interview. It lives in adverb form a lot: 꼼꼼하게 확인하다, 꼼꼼하게 챙기다. Two boundaries matter. First, don't confuse it with 깔끔하다, which is about being neat/tidy in appearance or finish; you can be 꼼꼼한 (thorough) without being 깔끔한, and vice versa. Second, its negative twin is 까다롭다 (picky/demanding to the point of being hard to satisfy) — when thoroughness tips into slowing everyone down, Koreans switch to 까다롭다. The English-speaker pitfall is the adverb: it is 꼼꼼하게 or 꼼꼼히, and you should not bolt 로 onto it (no 꼼꼼하게로); and as praise it modifies how someone works, so anchor it to a verb like 하다/확인하다 rather than leaving it bare.

Reaching for it when you mean 'fussy/hard to please' — that nuance is 까다롭다, not the complimentary 꼼꼼하다

usage: Also used for skin, allergies, stomach, sleep
examples: 나 요즘 좀 예민해.
I'm a bit on edge lately.
A quick, very natural heads-up to a friend; banmal
시험 기간이라 요즘 예민하니까 이해해 줘.
It's exam season so I'm on edge — please bear with me.
-(으)니까 gives the reason for asking forbearance
저는 잠귀가 예민해서 작은 소리에도 깨요.
I'm a light sleeper, so even small sounds wake me up.
잠귀가 예민하다 = sensitive ears while sleeping; the physical sense
nuance: 예민하다 covers two strands: a person being emotionally on-edge, touchy, or easily set off (usually from stress), and physical sensitivity — 피부 (skin), 잠귀 (sleep), 속/위 (stomach). It is Sino-Korean: 銳敏 (銳 sharp + 敏 quick/keen), literally 'sharply keen', which is why it reaches into both perception and temper. About someone's mood it can sound mildly critical, so people most often apply it to themselves as a pre-emptive warning. Two contrasts to fix: 민감하다 (also 'sensitive', 敏感) overlaps heavily but is the word of choice when an issue, market, or sensor is 'sensitive' (민감한 문제 = a sensitive matter), whereas a person on edge is more naturally 예민한; and 예리하다 (sharp/incisive, of a mind or analysis) is a false friend — it means perceptive, not irritable. The English trap is assuming 'sensitive = caring/tender'; for a gently sensitive, easily-moved heart, Koreans say 섬세하다, not 예민하다.

usage: 겉으로는 = on the outside, sets up a 'but inside…' turn
examples: 우리 아빠는 좀 무뚝뚝해.
My dad is kind of gruff.
A stock, affectionate description of Korean fathers; banmal
사장님이 무뚝뚝하게 대답해서 화난 줄 알았어요.
The boss answered so curtly that I thought he was angry.
-(으)ㄴ 줄 알았다 = mistakenly thought that…
우리 아빠는 무뚝뚝하지만 속은 정말 따뜻해요.
My dad is gruff but really warm on the inside.
속은 따뜻하다 = warm inside; the classic redeeming-turn collocation
nuance: 무뚝뚝하다 is native Korean describing a curt, unexpressive manner — short answers, no small talk, a flat face — without necessarily meaning the person is unkind. It is so reliably paired with 속은 따뜻하다 ('warm inside') that the 'gruff exterior, warm interior' arc is almost a cultural template for dads, older men, and Gyeongsang-do speakers. The crucial contrast is with 차갑다 (cold-hearted): 차갑다 implies the person actually is cold toward you, while 무뚝뚝하다 is only about an undemonstrative style — the feeling underneath may be perfectly warm. It also differs from 무례하다 (rude), which is a breach of manners; a 무뚝뚝한 person follows etiquette, they just don't decorate it with warmth. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: spelling (the syllable doubles — 무뚝뚝하다, not 무뚝하다), and resisting the instinct to read curtness as hostility, since Koreans hear it as personality, not an insult.

Equating it with 차갑다 (cold-hearted) — 무뚝뚝하다 is just an unexpressive style and often coexists with real warmth

usage: High compliment for a partner or close friend
have a warm way of speaking
다정다감 is a common four-syllable expansion
examples: 너 진짜 다정하다.
You're so sweet.
A warm, direct compliment to a friend; banmal
선생님이 다정하게 말해 줘서 긴장이 풀렸어요.
The teacher spoke to me so warmly that my nerves eased.
긴장이 풀리다 = tension eases; 다정하게 modifies how they spoke
남자친구가 너무 다정해서 친구들이 다 부러워해요.
My boyfriend is so sweet that all my friends are jealous.
부러워하다 = be envious; a real-life relationship boast
nuance: 다정하다 means warm, tender, and affectionate toward others — it is about emotional closeness and sweet treatment, which makes it the go-to compliment for partners, dear friends, and beloved teachers. It is Sino-Korean at the root: 多情 (多 many + 情 affection/feeling), literally 'much feeling', i.e. full of warmth. The dividing line that matters is with 친절하다 (kind/polite): 친절하다 is the right word for staff being helpful to a customer or a stranger giving directions — courteous service — whereas 다정하다 implies real, personal warmth, so it sounds slightly off for a one-time formal exchange. The expanded 다정다감하다 is a touch more literary but common in praise. The English trap is mapping 'nice/friendly' onto 다정하다 across the board: a cashier being pleasant is 친절한, not 다정한, and reserving 다정하다 for genuine warmth is what keeps it from sounding strange.

Applying it to a one-time formal stranger — it implies real intimacy, so it rings false there; use 친절하다
Confusing the adverb target: 다정하게 modifies how you treat/speak to someone (다정하게 대하다), so anchor it to a verb

usage: Mildly negative, but often said affectionately
be snippy today of all days
까칠하게 굴다 = behave in a prickly way
The original literal sense: rough to the touch
examples: 너 왜 이렇게 까칠해?
Why are you so snippy?
Casual concern between friends; banmal
우리 팀장님 평소엔 괜찮은데 마감 때만 까칠해져요.
Our team lead is usually fine but gets prickly only around deadlines.
마감 = deadline; -아/어지다 = become
그 사람 까칠해 보여도 알고 보면 착해요.
He seems prickly, but once you really get to know him he's nice.
알고 보면 = when you actually get to know
nuance: 까칠하다 literally means 'rough to the touch' (you'll still hear 피부가 까칠하다 for dry, stubbly skin) and figuratively describes someone snippy, easily irritated, or hard to please. Crucially it is fairly light and even playful — friends tease each other with it — so it is nowhere near a serious insult; for genuinely mean or nasty, Koreans say 못됐다. The contrast learners most need is with 까다롭다: 까다롭다 is about high, demanding standards (a 까다로운 손님 sends the dish back because it doesn't meet their bar), while 까칠하다 is about mood and attitude (a 까칠한 사람 is touchy and short with you regardless of standards). It very often appears with -아/어지다 to mark a temporary shift (마감 때 까칠해지다 = gets prickly at deadlines) and with 굴다 (까칠하게 굴다). The English-speaker pitfall is over-reading it as harsh: it's closer to 'a bit prickly/snippy' than to 'mean', so deploying it as a real insult overshoots.

usage: Encouraging a friend to speak up
Beloved set phrase for small, harmless payback
examples: 저 좀 소심해요.
I'm a bit timid.
Said with a self-deprecating laugh; the form is 소심해요, not 소심하해요
소심하게 굴지 말고 그냥 물어봐!
Don't be timid, just ask!
A friendly push to be bolder; 굴다 = behave/act
지각한 동료 자리에 몰래 포스트잇 붙였어. 소심한 복수지.
I secretly stuck a post-it on my late coworker's desk. Petty revenge.
소심한 복수 = the classic playful 'petty revenge' phrase
nuance: 소심하다 means timid, fainthearted, or easily intimidated — and unlike the neutral 내성적이다 ('introverted'), it leans negative, implying you hold back when you really shouldn't (can't send back a wrong dish, can't speak up in a meeting). It is Sino-Korean: 小心 (小 small + 心 heart), literally 'small-hearted'. Beware a false-friend trap here: the Chinese 小心 means 'be careful', but in Korean 소심하다 does NOT mean careful — it means timid; the 'careful/prudent' meaning belongs to 신중하다. The sharp contrast with 내성적이다 is the whole point: an introvert simply recharges alone, while a 소심한 person shrinks back out of fear, so the two are not interchangeable. The much-loved set phrase 소심한 복수 ('petty revenge') is everywhere. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the false friend, is using it as an interview 'strength' — it sounds self-critical, so pick 신중하다 (prudent) instead.

usage: wait in a relaxed, unhurried way
take it easy, relax one's mind
examples: 급할 거 없으니까 느긋하게 해.
There's no rush, so take your time.
급하다 = be in a hurry; a reassuring, soothing tone
저는 성격이 느긋해서 웬만한 일에는 스트레스를 안 받아요.
I'm laid-back, so most things don't stress me out.
웬만한 = most ordinary; 스트레스 받다 = get stressed
휴가 때는 느긋하게 늦잠도 자고 싶어요.
On vacation I want to sleep in and just take it easy.
늦잠 자다 = sleep in; 느긋하게 colors the whole leisure scene
nuance: 느긋하다 is native Korean for the positive flavor of 'laid-back' — calm, unbothered, and not easily rushed — and it works both for a person's temperament (성격이 느긋하다) and for relaxed stretches of time (느긋한 아침, 느긋한 주말). Its natural antonym is 급하다 (impatient/hasty), and the two are often set against each other. Two contrasts keep it precise. With 여유롭다 (which overlaps), 느긋하다 is about an unhurried temperament, while 여유롭다 leans toward having actual leeway — of time, space, or means (마음의 여유, 시간 여유); you can feel 느긋한 even when you're not objectively 여유로운. With 게으르다 (lazy), the difference is intent: 느긋하다 is unhurried by choice and still gets things done, whereas 게으르다 is an unwillingness to work — calling a relaxed person 게으른 is an insult, not a description. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that lazy/laid-back slip, plus the conjugation: it's a regular 하다-stem, so 느긋해요 / 느긋한, never 느긋어요.

usage: Also describes a room, class, or chat
examples: 저 아이는 진짜 활발하네요.
That kid is really lively.
A warm remark watching an energetic child; 활발하다 about visible energy
새로 온 인턴이 성격이 활발해서 금방 다 친해졌어요.
The new intern is so lively that everyone got close fast.
금방 = quickly; 친해지다 = get close
동아리에서 활발하게 활동하면 친구를 많이 사귈 수 있어요.
If you're active in a club, you can make lots of friends.
동아리 = club; 활발하게 활동하다 is a fixed pairing
nuance: 활발하다 describes lively, energetic, sociable behavior — it's how you praise someone bright and engaged in groups, and it stretches naturally to atmospheres and activities (활발한 토론 = a lively debate, 분위기가 활발하다 = the vibe is lively). It is Sino-Korean: 活潑 (活 alive + 潑 to splash/be spirited), literally 'alive and splashing', a vivid image of bubbling energy. The contrast that matters is with 외향적이다: 외향적이다 names the inner MBTI-style trait (where you draw energy), while 활발하다 names the observable liveliness in the moment — a true extrovert who's exhausted simply won't look 활발한 right then, and a normally reserved person can be 활발한 at a party they love. It's almost always a compliment about people. The English-speaker pitfall is using it as a flat synonym for 'outgoing/extroverted'; reserve 활발하다 for visible energy and motion, and don't attach it to calm, inanimate things, where it sounds wrong.

examples: 목소리가 참 차분하시네요.
You have such a calm voice.
A polite compliment using honorific -(으)시-; about composure, not volume
차 한 잔 마시니까 마음이 좀 차분해졌어요.
After a cup of tea my mind calmed down a bit.
-(으)니까 marks the natural cause; 차분해지다 = grow calm
급한 상황에서도 차분하게 대처해서 다들 놀랐어요.
Even in an urgent situation they handled it calmly, so everyone was impressed.
대처하다 = handle/respond to; a strong interview-worthy trait
nuance: 차분하다 is native Korean for calm, composed, and steady — a person who doesn't get rattled, or a quiet, settled mood. It is a strong compliment, especially for keeping your head under pressure (차분하게 대처하다), which makes it an excellent trait to claim in interviews. It commonly takes -아/어지다 to mark a shift into calm (마음이 차분해지다). The contrast learners need most is with 조용하다 (quiet): 조용하다 is about low sound/volume — a quiet room or a person who simply doesn't talk much — while 차분하다 is about inner composure and temperament; someone can speak up plenty and still be 차분한. It also sits opposite 예민하다 (on-edge) and 급하다 (hasty). The English-speaker pitfalls are mapping 'calm = quiet' onto it (they diverge — composure vs. volume) and the conjugation: it's a regular 하다-adjective, so 차분해요 / 차분한, never the doubled 차분하해요.

usage: Not noticing details or others' moods
무심하게 = without thinking much of it
look after someone in a low-key way
Trendy phrase: aloof on the surface, caring underneath
examples: 남편이 좀 무심해요.
My husband is kind of inattentive.
An extremely common, half-joking relationship complaint
친구가 무심하게 던진 말에 상처받았어요.
I got hurt by something my friend said offhandedly.
무심하게 던진 말 = a careless, throwaway remark
그 선배는 무심한 듯 챙겨 줘서 인기가 많아요.
That senior looks aloof but quietly looks out for people, so they're popular.
무심한 듯 챙기다 = the beloved 'cold but caring' type
nuance: 무심하다 means indifferent, aloof, or simply not paying attention to others' feelings and small changes — it's the stock (half-joking) complaint about a partner who never notices a new haircut. It is Sino-Korean: 無心 (無 without + 心 heart/mind), literally 'without mind/heart', i.e. not having one's attention on something. Importantly it is gentler than 차갑다 (cold-hearted): a 무심한 person may genuinely care but just fails to show it or notice, whereas 차갑다 implies real emotional coldness toward you — which is exactly why the trendy praise 무심한 듯 챙기다 ('caring in a seemingly indifferent way') works. The other contrast is 무관심하다 (無關心, 'no interest'), which is stronger and usually aimed at topics or matters (정치에 무관심하다 = uninterested in politics), while 무심하다 is about a person's inattentive disposition toward people. The English-speaker pitfall is sliding to 'cold' or 'doesn't care at all'; 무심하다 is closer to 'doesn't notice / doesn't show it' than to genuine coldness or total disinterest.
